newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Fuel prices drive air fares up by 3 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Fuel prices drive air fares up by 3 pct.

text.p: The world's airlines on Friday proposed a global three percent passenger fare increase to make up for a surge of more than 40 percent in fuel costs this year, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) said.
The 251-member airlines body said the proposed increase, which is subject to government approvals, would apply to fares from December 15.
"The proposed increase in fares...will go some way to contributing to the restoration of profitability for the airlines industry," IATA said in a statement.
The decision came after three days of closed-door discussions on the issue at IATA's Geneva headquarters.

Head of IATA's tariff affairs, Patrick Murphy, told Reuters the proposal was in response to a rise in 1996 of more than 40 percent in fuel prices, which account for 10 percent of most airlines' costs.

Some European carriers have already announced ticket price hikes so there would be exceptions in Europe and some rises would be lower, he said. Other exceptions included Greece and Canada, which had proposed a five percent increase each.
IATA said the average price of aviation fuel was 73.2 cents a gallon based on spot world prices in October, up from 53.6 cents in June and compared with 51.3 cents in October 1995.
This meant a 43 percent year-on-year increase, it said.
Many European carriers were pushing for a concerted move on lift ticket prices by up to three per cent, but Asian and North American ones were believed to be reluctant to do so.

Last week IATA Director-General Pierre Jeanniot told top airline executives attending the body's annual general meeting that collectively they were heading for their second year in a row of record profits.
But, partly due to the fuel price rise, he reduced an earlier profit estimate to $5.5 billion from $6 billion.
The rise in the cost of jet fuel this year has especially hit some of the less profitable airlines.

Finland's Finnair indicated on Tuesday it wanted an increase to be agreed at the Geneva meeting, and Scandivanian airline SAS announced a two-per cent increase for passengers and five per cent for cargo to go into effect on Friday.

Even highly successful carriers say they are suffering. British Airways reported last week that despite strong traffic growth and greater productivity its first half operating profits were down 2.1 per cent compared with last year.
Part of the drop, it said, was due to the extra $84 million it had had to pay for fuel.
Germany's Lufthansa, which said last week it had paid an extra $67 million in fuel prices so far this year, was reported on Thursday to be heading for a 1996 profit only close to last year's result.

Last year, airlines paid an average worldwide price for fuel of 65.2 U.S. cents a gallon (4.5 litres). After a steady rise this year, fuel leapt to 77.5 cents a gallon in September amid new tension in the Gulf.
